state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's focus on the misconception that changing all values by the same proportion wouldn't affect the range. Think about how changing all the plant heights by the same amount would impact the difference between the tallest and shortest plant. Can you see how the range would actually change in this scenario?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Hmm, so when Katie adds 3 cm to all of them, the difference between the tallest and shortest would still be the same because you're adding the same amount to both? But then why would Tom be right about cutting them in half - wouldn't that change the range too if we're dividing everything by the same number?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: You're on the right track with the idea of adding the same amount to each height not changing the range. When cutting the heights in half, think about how the ratios of the heights would change and how that would affect the range. Can you see how dividing by the same number would impact the range differently than adding the same amount?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher directly addresses the proportional change misconception and the student shows clear progress by Turn 2 in understanding that adding maintains range while dividing changes it, though the teacher's scaffolding could have been more concrete given the student's initial confusion.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher uses guided questioning to lead the student to discover the answer rather than directly explaining with worked examples, which is inconsistent with the traditional strategy of explicit instruction.
